papers.title: Is Prosody Encoded in the Neural Audio Codec Mimi?
papers.abstract: Neural audio codecs (NACs) have become a fundamental infrastructure for modern speech-language models, discretizing continuous speech signals into token sequences that enable large language models to process and generate audio. Most research evaluates codec quality at the decoding phase, assessing the naturalness of reconstructed speech. However, little research investigates what phonetic information is captured during encoding. In this paper, we investigated the potential correlates of prosody in the NAC Mimi, a codec used by conversational speech agents such as Moshi and Sesame and used in downstream tasks such as speech-to-speech translation (Hibiki).

papers.title: Do Layer Rankings Survive Silence Trimming? The Silence Shortcut in Frozen WavLM Representations for Audio Deepfake Detection
papers.abstract: Layer-wise analyses of frozen self-supervised encoders are used to locate spoofing information in audio deepfake detection. On the ASVspoof 2019 logical access (LA) benchmark, bonafide recordings carry longer leading and trailing silence than spoofed ones, and detectors exploit this cue, the silence shortcut. This paper examines whether layer rankings for a frozen WavLM Base encoder survive the trimming of this silence. A small classifier is trained on each of the 12 layers with and without trimming and evaluated on ASVspoof 2019 LA and, zero-shot, on In-the-Wild, in all four train/test combinations, with speaker-level bootstrap intervals. Trimming at 40 dB raises the in-domain error at every layer and preserves the layer ranking only partly (Kendall's tau of 0.58 in domain, 0.73-0.76 on In-the-Wild). The best layer is unchanged at 40 dB, but on the evaluation set it moves from layer 5 to layer 6 at 15 dB and, with mean pooling, at 20 dB, thresholds at which trimming may also remove low-energy speech. At 40 dB, the equal error rate of a model trained with silence rises by 6.3-19.9 percentage points at every layer when only its test audio is trimmed. On In-the-Wild, the effect depends on the layer: at layers 3-5, trimming the test audio lowers the error only for models trained on trimmed audio, whereas at layers 6, 8, and 9 training on trimmed audio lowers it also on clean test audio. We quantify how zero padding alters WavLM features through group normalization, an effect that an attention mask does not fully undo.

papers.title: ClusterVAD: Threshold-Free Unsupervised Voice Activity Detection with Pre-Trained Neural Representations
papers.abstract: Voice activity detection (VAD) is one of the first steps in speech processing pipelines, from transcription and diarization to speech language models. Supervised detectors need labelled data and inherit the domain and annotation conventions of their training corpora. Existing unsupervised detectors rely on hand-crafted acoustic features which cannot benefit from data and degrade in far-field, noisy or atypical speech. We propose ClusterVAD, an unsupervised VAD built on frozen speech foundation model representations. Fitted once on a small set of untranscribed speech, it clusters the representations and labels each cluster as speech or non-speech with sonority, an acoustic measure. At inference, a frame-level speech probability is computed from the cluster assignments, and a two-state hidden Markov model fitted to each recording enables threshold-free detection. Across benchmarks covering meetings, far-field and noisy recordings, Mandarin and dysarthric speech, ClusterVAD obtains the lowest detection error on pause-level references and is competitive on speaker turn-level references. These results indicate that speech foundation models inherently capture the distinction between speech and non-speech, which can be leveraged without training a detector.

papers.title: Perfect Scores, Misplaced Explanations: A Controlled Study of Explainability in Audio Deepfake Detection
papers.abstract: What if an explanation achieves perfect scores but it is uninterpretable? We show that this happens when explaining audio deepfake detectors. Using an optimization-based method, we explain a state-of-the-art wav2vec2-based detector. The explanations achieve optimal scores on standard explainability metrics, i.e. fidelity and faithfulness. Visual inspection, however, reveals unintuitive and uninterpretable patterns. To understand this discrepancy, we run a controlled perturbation study in which we modify known frequency regions of the speech signal. Although we propose a model that is able to obtain close-to-optimal results with respect to the metrics, the explanations locate the manipulated region only when it is fixed across samples, and mostly fall to chance level when it varies. We further show that the signal used to fill the removed regions largely determines the explanation and its localization, without being reflected in the metrics.

papers.title: MADlibs: Analyzing the Distribution of Generative Music
papers.abstract: What music can a text-to-music model actually make? The answer to this question has consequences for individual creators, communities, and musical culture more broadly. We introduce MADlibs, a framework to measure the expressive support of state-of-the-art music generators: the subset of musical behaviors they will actually produce across the space of prompts. We first develop strategies for generating musical prompts using natural language processing methods and existing caption corpora. Then, we use a set of MIR techniques to study the corresponding output spaces in terms of interpretable and qualitatively meaningful elements like key, beat, tempo, instrumentation, and dynamics. We find that text-to-music models are not interchangeable instruments for the same prompt space. Rather, each model has learned idiosyncratic properties that constrain the regime of music reachable via prompting it, for example, defaulting to certain tempi, failing to produce silences, or oversampling canonical band arrangements. Because users interact with these systems one prompt at a time, these biases are often invisible in practice yet cumulatively shape what AI-assisted music sounds like, risking the production of a new auditory monoculture hidden behind the promise of universal describability. We thus urge the MIR community to further study and responsibly steer population-level properties of music generation models.

papers.title: VividAudio: Multi-Event Reference-Conditioned Video-to-Audio Generation
papers.abstract: Existing video-to-audio (V2A) methods have achieved promising results in synthesizing high-quality audios. However, as V2A advances toward more flexible user-directed creation, existing methods remain notably limited in controlling the distinct acoustic identities of multiple events within a video. We therefore formulate multi-event reference-conditioned V2A (Mr-V2A), where each event is assigned a specific audio reference and target time span. Mr-V2A presents three key challenges. First, event-level reference-target training pairs are scarce. We introduce Intra-Video Event Variation (IntraEvtVar), which constructs non-oracle pairs through four variation modes of events mined within each video. Second, we organize the references into a Time-Aligned COmposite Reference (TACO-Ref) and inject it through local and global pathways: the local pathway retains time-resolved event cues, while an Audio Q-Former provides a clip-level acoustic-context condition. Third, jointly conditioning on multiple references can cause acoustic-attribute leakage across events. Localized reference attention and the TACO-Ref Router (TRR) explicitly constrain event-to-reference correspondence to reduce such interference. Experiments on VGGSound-Ref and VividBench demonstrate stronger reference controllability than existing V2A and exemplar-based methods while maintaining competitive Foley generation quality.

papers.title: HEAR, SEE, SPIKE ONCE: Highly Efficient NeuroAI Temporal Neural Networks for Low-Precision Multimodal Audio-Visual Classification and Online Learning
papers.abstract: Spiking neural networks for multimodal audio-visual classification reach high accuracy by adopting deep-learning machinery: multi-stage convolutional or transformer encoders trained end-to-end with surrogate-gradient backpropagation through time. These prior works typically rely on full-precision (32-bit) parameters and do not treat hardware efficiency as a primary design objective. In this paper, we propose NeuTNN-AV, a much simpler hardware-amenable multimodal substrate built on the recently proposed NeuroAI Temporal Neural Network (NeuTNN) and demonstrate that it can match or outperform state-of-the-art SNN baselines with a fraction of their synapse counts. NeuTNN neurons carry multiple active dendritic segments. Each input line spikes at most once (temporal coding) and every weight is learned via a local reward-modulated spike-timing dependent plasticity (STDP) rule. All weights are 4-bit integers and inference uses only comparisons and additions. On CREMA-D, it reaches 78.6% with 2.34M synapses establishing a new state-of-the-art SNN accuracy, against 77.14% for MISNet-XL (31M parameters). On UrbanSound8K-AV, NeuTNN reaches 98.82% with 1.38M synapses, against 96.85% for SMMT (9.99M parameters) and 98.96% for MISNet-XL (31M parameters). Weight memory is 23-106x smaller than the spiking baselines, and the measured synaptic energy per inference is two to three orders of magnitude lower. Furthermore, the proposed NeuTNN learns CREMA-D in a single pass with 73.8% accuracy and demonstrates rapid online continual learning by adapting to unseen actors from a few dozen clips.

papers.title: Phoneme-identity depth profiles do not reliably predict LoRA placement for dysarthric ASR
papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient adaptation of a speech foundation model to dysarthric speech requires a rarely justified choice: which encoder layers to adapt. A recently proposed strategy is to probe the encoder, find where phonetic information becomes most decodable, and put the adapters there. We test that inference across two ASR models (Qwen3-ASR, Whisper-small) and two dysarthric corpora (Mandarin CDSD, English UASpeech), holding recipe and seed discipline constant. The inference fails. Measured under one pipeline rather than inherited from published figures, all four phoneme-error curves minimise between 83% and 92% of relative depth, each model's minimising layer moving no further between corpora than between probe seeds. The best adaptation band is not similarly constant: none of three natural mappings from the curve to a band -- steepest improvement, lowest band-mean error, or knee location -- recovers the best tested configuration. We do not claim no statistic of the curve could work, only that these three do not. Placement still matters, but is model- and corpus-specific. On CDSD the models disagree -- Qwen3-ASR prefers its upper third (29.88% CER, three-seed mean), Whisper-small all-block LoRA (53.56%) -- while on UASpeech neither favours the upper band. At three seeds, upper-versus-all is resolved (-1.31 pp, CI [-2.16, -0.25]) but upper-versus-middle is not (-0.83 pp, CI [-2.06, +1.86]). The two models' preferences differ as a directly tested interaction (-4.71 pp, CI [-6.17, -2.89]); we designate this the primary claim, and record that the designation was made post hoc. On Qwen3-ASR x UASpeech, adapting near the input is reliably worse than not adapting at all (+9.90 pp CER). We recommend choosing the band by a short adaptation sweep on the model and corpus in hand, not by reading it off a probe.

papers.title: Putting a Robot on a Phone Call: Layered Signaling, Bounded Occupancy and Turn Arbitration over WebRTC
papers.abstract: We put a Thor robot on a browser voice call, with speech sent from Safari, answers played through the robot's loudspeaker and transcripts returned to the phone. We separate HTTPS signaling, relayed WebRTC media and speech generation into independently observable routes. The browser prefetches relay credentials and allows a 500 ms window after its first relay candidate. The backend starts speech and WebRTC-answer preparation concurrently within a 55 s deadline. A session slot and a non-blocking speaker lock coordinate calls with local voice access. A 2 s gate gives the controller an opportunity to suppress chat before playback. Fifteen of sixteen first dials reached ready-to-speak, comprising seven of eight Wi-Fi calls with a median of 5.57 s and eight of eight cellular calls with a median of 6.76 s. All twenty scored occupancy and recovery scenarios admitted a later call. During five 60 s outages, the backend released the line while the phone remained offline. Across 40 controlled replays, enabling the gate suppressed chat when the controller decided at 1 s. At 3 s, chat and controller feedback both played in sequence, with no overlapping output in any trace. Two additional boundary traces exposed a receipt naming a later feedback item and a new call's query returning its predecessor's feedback. These measurements cover application events on one platform and simulated controller decisions, with acoustic output and task correctness outside their scope.

papers.title: The crisis of digital truth: deepfakes and normative disruption in algorithmic society
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence has made deepfakes a source of instability in contemporary information environments, challenging not only communication processes but also the normative arrangements through which trust, evidence, and accountability are established. This article examines their implications for digital societies and conceptualizes them as a form of normative disruption. A structured conceptual synthesis of research in political communication, social epistemology, platform studies, and law was combined with a functional comparison of emerging regulatory frameworks. A diagnostic application to the 2023 Slovak election audio deepfake illustrates the resulting framework without claiming empirical validation. The analysis develops PROVE, a five-dimensional model of normative resilience comprising Provenance, Responsibility, Observability, Verification, and Epistemic resilience. The Slovak case highlights interactions among weak provenance, fragmented responsibility, restricted observability, time-sensitive verification, and public trust. Transparency, labeling, and detection are necessary but insufficient when synthetic media also facilitate strategic denial and cross-platform recirculation. Effective governance requires an integrated architecture supporting technical provenance, distributed accountability, platform observability, institutional verification, and public epistemic resilience. PROVE offers a diagnostic framework for assessing institutional vulnerabilities and guiding future comparative research, rather than a previously validated measurement scale.

papers.title: Who Plays What: Same-Instrument Music Separation from Video
papers.abstract: When two musicians in an ensemble play the same instrument, they sound alike and their instruments look alike. Audio-only separators, and audio-visual separators that rely on appearance, cannot tell them apart. What still differs is how each player moves, and when. We study same-instrument per-player separation: a user clicks one musician in a video and receives that musician's sound alone, even when other players in the video play the same instrument. Our model follows the clicked player and describes them with high level video features and the velocities of body and hand keypoints. A pretrained music separator attends to these tokens through cross-attention. Earlier motion-based separators were scored only on synthetic mixtures of solo videos. We give the first per-player evaluation of same-instrument separation on real ensemble recordings. On 58 players in URMP, each sharing an instrument with at least one other player in the piece, our model reaches a median SDR of 5.3 dB, while four released separators, audio-only and audio-visual, stay at or below 0.3 dB. The gap is wider on same-instrument duets, and our model also beats the audio-visual baselines on their own MUSIC benchmark. Tests show that the gain comes from movement: replacing the video with a still frame removes it, and so does shifting the video by a fraction of a second against the audio.
reasons: Evaluation, Alignment, Safety & Copyright: music benchmark

papers.title: PopMelodyGen: A Copyright-Aware Platform for Controllable Pop-Melody Generation
papers.abstract: Large-scale redistributable symbolic pop-melody data remain scarce due to copyright restrictions, creating a bottleneck for both practical deployment and reproducible research in music generation. We present PopMelodyGen, a copyright-aware platform for controllable pop-melody generation that combines rule-based synthesis with neural generation. Our approach first uses an expert synthesizer to produce large-scale labeled synthetic melodies from explicit musical knowledge and templates, providing scalable pretraining data with auditable provenance. A neural model is then pretrained on this corpus and adapted with a small licensed real-pop corpus to improve melodic naturalness while preserving controllability. The platform supports interactive melody creation with accompaniment playback and export for creators, as well as batch construction of annotated symbolic datasets for researchers. PopMelodyGen demonstrates a practical training and deployment paradigm for creative AI when large-scale reusable real-world data are limited.
papers.venue: AAAI 2027 Demonstration Program (accepted); extended version with appendix

# ADA Omni — Open-Source Local Turkish Speech-to-Speech Voice AI (Single-Architecture Omni, 12 GB GPU)

> **Built with Gemma** — ADA Omni (`urbanhorizons/ada-omni-tr`) is an open-source, fully local **Turkish Audio-to-Audio Streaming Voice AI** that runs on a single consumer **12 GB NVIDIA RTX 3060** (or 8 GB GPU with `--low_vram`) with **~0.86–1.40 s** end-to-end latency, **24 kHz** natural Turkish speech, `< 80 ms` barge-in interruption, native `"Ada"` wake-word gating, voiceprint speaker recognition, and plug-and-play `@register_tool` IoT/agent tools — with **zero external Whisper/ASR** and **zero disconnected text-to-TTS pipeline**.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Scope & Safety Notice:** This repository is an open-source research and personal/smart-home voice-assistant reference architecture. It is **NOT** a medical device, clinical advisor, or emergency call system. Do not use it for unsupervised life-critical or safety-critical decisions.

---

---

## Why ADA Omni? (Traditional ASR+LLM+TTS Pipeline vs. ADA Omni)

| Feature | Traditional Turkish Pipeline (`Whisper → LLM → TTS`) | **ADA Omni (`urbanhorizons/ada-omni-tr`)** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Audio Understanding** | External ASR (Whisper) loses tone & adds latency | **Native Gemma-3n USM Audio Tower** (zero external ASR) |
| **Brain → Mouth Link** | Disconnected plain-text string handoff | **Lossless (`Cos=1.00`) cross-vocab embedding alignment + `20 MB` Gemma-3n Prosody/Emotion Bridge (`v2.0`)** |
| **Voice Quality** | Often flat/robotic or metallic on local models | **24 kHz natural Turkish** (frozen `0.6B` 12.5 Hz RVQ-16 codec) |
| **First-Audio Latency** | Typically `3.0 – 6.0 s` | **`~0.86 – 1.40 s`** on RTX 3060 (Dual CUDA Graph) |
| **Interruption (Barge-In)** | Usually half-duplex / sluggish | **`< 80 ms` instant barge-in** + `"Ada"` native wake-word |
| **Voice Customization** | Retraining required | **Zero-shot 5-second `--ref_wav`** (Apache-2.0 female/male included) |

---

## Architecture
```text
[Raw Microphone Audio (16 kHz)]
        │  (No external Whisper / ASR)
        ▼
[Gemma-3n-E2B USM Audio Tower + Brain]   ──► CUDA Graph (~40.1 tok/s on RTX 3060)
        │  (Token IDs + internal last_hidden_state prosody vectors)
        ▼
[ExactBaseProsodyBridge (20 MB, v2.0)]   ──► Lossless (Cos=1.00) cross-vocab base + L2-regularized Conv1D prosody residual
        │
        ▼
[Frozen 0.6B Talker + 5-layer CodePredictor + 12.5 Hz Decoder] ──► CUDA Graph (~180–210 ms TTFA, RTF 0.37x)
        │  ◄── Apache-2.0 open-source speaker embedding (or custom 5s --ref_wav)
        ▼
[24 kHz Streaming Turkish Speech + <80 ms Barge-In]
```

---

## Real Reproducible Benchmarks & Training Metrics

### 1. Hardware Latency & Memory (Measured — No Synthetic Estimates)
| Hardware | Brain (`Gemma-3n`) | Mouth (`0.6B` 12.5 Hz) | End-to-End First Audio | Memory |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **RTX 3060 12 GB (Dual CUDA Graph)** | `40.1 tok/s` (`24.9 ms/tok`) | `180–210 ms` TTFA, **`RTF 0.37x`** | **`~0.86 – 1.40 s`** | `10.0–10.6 GB VRAM` |
| **8 GB RTX GPU (`--low_vram` mode)** | Eager + CPU PLE | `~205 ms` TTFA, **`RTF 0.37x`** | `~2.5 – 4.0 s` | `~7.8 GB VRAM` |
| **CPU-Only (Ryzen 5 5500, PyTorch INT8)** | `4.86 tok/s` | `RTF 4.17x` *(not real-time)* | `~6.5 s` *(stutters)* | `~16 GB RAM` |

### 2. Bridge Alignment, v2.0 Changelog & Endurance Metrics
- **v2.0 Architecture Upgrade (`ExactBaseProsodyBridge`, `20.02 MB`):** Replaced v1.0/v1.1's lossy MLP vocabulary approximation (`Cos = 0.89–0.90`, which occasionally slurred multi-syllable words) with **lossless (`Cos = 1.00`) cross-vocab embedding lookup** fused with an L2-regularized (`delta_l2 = 0.30`) Conv1D prosody/emotion residual trained on `10,000` conversational Turkish clips (`0.6B` 100% frozen).
- **Held-Out Validation (`200` unseen conversational Turkish clips):** Dropped from `VAL c0_CE = 1.4526 (55.2%)` at step 0 (flat exact base) to **`VAL c0_CE = 1.2358 (59.8%)`**, `VAL sub_Depth_CE = 5.0159` (`dRMS = 0.1556`), with CUDA-Graph-safe `top_k = 30` sampling (`temp = 0.62`).
- **1-Click Installer & Runtime Auto-Patches (`v2.0`):** Added `install.bat` (Windows) and `install.sh` (Linux) plus automatic `transformers==4.53.3` ↔ `qwen-tts==0.1.1` compatibility shims (`runtime_patches.py`), verified end-to-end on a fresh `git clone` + `venv` (`9.96 GB VRAM`, `TTFA 174–217 ms`, `RTF 0.37–0.43x`).
- **Voice Disentanglement (`F0` pitch verification):** Same `20.02 MB` bridge yields `222–295 Hz` (Apache-2.0 female ref, `prosody_scale = 1.0`) and `99.5–133 Hz` (Apache-2.0 male ref, `prosody_scale = 0.55`) with zero gender drift.
- **100-Turn Continuous Live Stress Test:** `100 / 100` consecutive turns completed with **`0` crashes** and **`0` OOMs**.

---

## Key Features
- **Native `"Ada"` Wake Word + 25s Active Window (`0 MB` Extra VRAM):** Ignores background TV and room conversations until addressed with `"Ada"`, then keeps a 25-second natural follow-up window.
- **Voiceprint Speaker Identification & Per-User Audio Memory (`0 MB` Extra VRAM):** Reuses the loaded `1024-D` speaker encoder (`~8 ms`) to identify household members by voice and keep per-user multi-turn audio history.
- **Plug-and-Play Modular Tools (`tools_registry.py`):** Register smart-home / MQTT / Home Assistant / API tools with `@register_tool(...)` — zero retraining. Includes device fault reporting, salted `PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256` passphrase protection (`ADA_OMNI_PASSPHRASE`) with 3-strike lockout, and zero-idle-RAM on-demand time/weather/web lookup.
- **Automatic Runtime Compatibility Patches (`runtime_patches.py`):** Automatically patches `transformers==4.53.3` Gemma-3n CUDA Graph blockers at runtime so fresh installs work out of the box.

---

## Installation & Quickstart (1-Click Setup)
**Prerequisites:** NVIDIA GPU (Ampere+ / BF16, CUDA 12.x, `>= 8 GB` VRAM; `12 GB` recommended) and `git-lfs`. On Linux: `sudo apt install libportaudio2 libsndfile1`.

```bash
git clone https://huggingface.co/urbanhorizons/ada-omni-tr
cd ada-omni-tr

# 1-Click Installer (creates venv + installs deps + CUDA PyTorch 2.5.1 + qwen-tts + verifies CUDA):
# Windows:
install.bat
# Linux:
bash install.sh

# Optional: set your own passphrase for protected tools (e.g., voice profile enrollment)
export ADA_OMNI_PASSPHRASE="your secret phrase"   # PowerShell: $env:ADA_OMNI_PASSPHRASE="your secret phrase"

# 12 GB+ GPU (Dual CUDA Graph, ~1s latency, wake-word "Ada" active):
.\venv\Scripts\python.exe ada_canli_mikrofon.py --voice kadin      # Linux: ./venv/bin/python ...
.\venv\Scripts\python.exe ada_canli_mikrofon.py --voice erkek
.\venv\Scripts\python.exe ada_canli_mikrofon.py --ref_wav my_custom_voice.wav

# 8 GB GPU mode (~7.8 GB VRAM):
.\venv\Scripts\python.exe ada_canli_mikrofon.py --voice kadin --low_vram
```

---

## Sık Sorulan Sorular (FAQ — Türkçe & English)

**Türkiye'de açık kaynak, yerel (offline) çalışan Türkçe Omni / Speech-to-Speech sesli yapay zekâ var mı?**  
Evet. **ADA Omni (`urbanhorizons/ada-omni-tr`)**, harici Whisper/ASR veya kopuk TTS boru hattı olmadan tek bir 12 GB RTX 3060 ekran kartında yerel olarak çalışan, 24 kHz doğal Türkçe konuşan, söz kesme (`< 80 ms`) ve `"Ada"` uyanma kelimesi destekli açık kaynak bir sesli yapay zekâ mimarisidir.

**Can ADA Omni run on CPU only (without a GPU)?**  
No, real-time speech streaming requires an NVIDIA GPU (`>= 8 GB` VRAM). On a 6-core Ryzen 5 5500 CPU with PyTorch INT8, real-time factor is `4.17x` (not real-time).

**Is this Moshi-style simultaneous full-duplex?**  
No — to be transparent, it is **Practical Full-Duplex (Hands-Free Streaming + `< 80 ms` Barge-In)**: Ada stops immediately when interrupted and then listens to your new utterance rather than decoding overlapping speech simultaneously.

---

## Known Limitations
1. **Practical Duplex (Barge-In), Not Simultaneous Overlapping Speech:** Stops in `< 80 ms` on interruption, then listens to the new turn.
2. **2B Backbone Reasoning Ceiling:** Under heavy noise, `Gemma-3n-E2B` can occasionally miss complex mental arithmetic.
3. **Speaker ID Is Convenience, Not Cryptographic Auth:** Cosine voiceprint matching (`0.72`) is for household personalization; sensitive tools require `ADA_OMNI_PASSPHRASE`.

# TBI TTS: English Text-to-Speech and Voice Cloning Model

**TBI TTS** is an English **text-to-speech (TTS)** model with **zero-shot voice cloning**, built by **[The Brihaspati Infotech](https://www.brihaspatitech.com/)**.
Give it a 10–20 second voice clip and any English text, and it speaks the text in that voice, with no extra training.
We fine-tuned it on a curated indian English speech dataset for clear, natural narration.

## Highlights

- **Clone a voice from seconds of audio.** One 10–20 second clip is enough.
- **Clear, accurate speech.** 99.3% word accuracy in our benchmark (0.66% word error rate); 75 of 80 test clips were transcribed word for word.
- **Measurably improved by our fine-tuning.** Word error rate fell from 1.15% to 0.66%, and estimated speech quality (PESQ) rose from 3.05 to 3.54.
- **Fast.** About 4× faster than real time on a single consumer GPU (NVIDIA RTX 4060 Ti).
- **Lightweight.** 337 million parameters; generation needs under 2 GB of GPU memory.
- **24 kHz audio**, Safetensors weights and a one-line command-line tool.

## Samples

| # | What it shows | Text | Audio |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Short sentence | "Welcome! This voice was generated by our custom fine tuned text to speech model." | <audio controls src="https://huggingface.co/mrinaltbi/tbi-tts/resolve/main/samples/sample1.wav"></audio> |
| 2 | Technical vocabulary | "Today we will look at how a power converter controls the voltage across its output." | <audio controls src="https://huggingface.co/mrinaltbi/tbi-tts/resolve/main/samples/sample2.wav"></audio> |
| 3 | Natural pacing | "Thanks for listening. Give it a short voice clip and any text, and it will read the text aloud in that voice." | <audio controls src="https://huggingface.co/mrinaltbi/tbi-tts/resolve/main/samples/sample3.wav"></audio> |
| 4 | Long-form narration (32 s) | "Welcome to this short lesson on renewable energy. Solar panels convert sunlight directly into electricity, while wind turbines capture the energy of moving air. Both sources are clean, but their output changes with the weather. That is why modern power grids combine them with storage systems, such as large batteries, to keep the supply steady throughout the day and night." | <audio controls src="https://huggingface.co/mrinaltbi/tbi-tts/resolve/main/samples/sample4.wav"></audio> |
| 5 | A different voice | "Every voice is unique, and with just a few seconds of audio, this model can speak in a new one." | <audio controls src="https://huggingface.co/mrinaltbi/tbi-tts/resolve/main/samples/sample5.wav"></audio> |

All samples are unedited model output (volume-normalized only), cloned from short reference clips of speakers in our training data.

## Model details

| | |
|---|---|
| Developed by | The Brihaspati Infotech |
| Model type | Zero-shot text-to-speech with voice cloning |
| Architecture | Diffusion Transformer (22 layers, 1,024 hidden size, 16 attention heads) trained with conditional flow matching |
| Parameters | 337 million |
| Output | 24 kHz mono audio; 100-band mel spectrogram decoded by a Vocos vocoder |
| Language | English |
| Text input | Character-level tokenizer (2,546 symbols) |
| Inputs | Reference clip (10–20 s; the model uses up to 12 s, trimmed at a natural pause), its transcript (optional; it can be transcribed automatically), and the text to speak |
| License | CC BY-NC 4.0 (non-commercial use) |

## Training data

| | |
|---|---|
| Content | English speech on engineering, science, mathematics and economics topics |
| Speakers | Multiple speakers with Indian English accents |
| Clip length | 1.0–19.1 seconds (median 2.5 s) |
| Preparation | Audio split into short clips, each paired with its transcript and filtered for quality |
| Format | 24 kHz mono audio with English transcripts |

## Training procedure

| | |
|---|---|
| Starting point | Pretrained multilingual base model (see Credits) |
| Audio processed during training | About 267 hours (36 passes over the data) |
| Batch size | Up to 2,000 mel frames (about 21 seconds of audio) per step |
| Optimizer | AdamW, learning rate 1e-5 with 100 warm-up steps, gradient clipping at 1.0 |
| Precision | fp16 mixed precision |
| Released weights | Exponential moving average (EMA) of the model weights |

## Evaluation

We tested on 20 new English sentences that are not in the training data (business, customer service, education, science and everyday topics),
each spoken in 4 reference voices of speakers from our dataset: 80 clips per model, with the same random seeds and settings (32 sampling steps) for both models.

| Model | Word accuracy ↑ | Perfect clips ↑ | Speaker similarity ↑ | Est. PESQ ↑ | Est. STOI ↑ | Est. SI-SDR ↑ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **TBI TTS (this model)** | **99.3%** | **75 / 80 (94%)** | **0.973** | **3.54** | **0.978** | **20.6 dB** |
| Base model before fine-tuning | 98.9% | 72 / 80 (90%) | 0.970 | 3.05 | 0.958 | 16.2 dB |

Word accuracy is 100% minus the word error rate (TBI TTS: 0.66%; base model: 1.15%).
We also ran the test with 64 sampling steps: TBI TTS scored the same (0.66% word error rate), so the faster default of 32 steps is recommended.
Both models run at the same speed: a real-time factor of 0.25, about 4× faster than real time, on one RTX 4060 Ti.

How we measured:
- **Word accuracy:** the generated audio is transcribed by Whisper large-v3-turbo and compared word by word with the input text.
- **Speaker similarity:** cosine similarity between WavLM-base-plus-SV speaker embeddings of the output and the reference clip (higher means closer to the target voice).
- **PESQ, STOI and SI-SDR:** no-reference estimates of speech quality, intelligibility and clarity from TorchAudio SQUIM.
- **Real-time factor:** generation time divided by audio length (below 1 is faster than real time).

## How to use

```bash
pip install f5-tts
huggingface-cli download mrinaltbi/tbi-tts --local-dir tbi-tts

f5-tts_infer-cli --model F5TTS_v1_Base \
  --ckpt_file tbi-tts/model.safetensors \
  --vocab_file tbi-tts/vocab.txt \
  --ref_audio reference.wav \
  --ref_text "Exact transcript of the reference clip." \
  --gen_text "Text you want spoken."
```

Python:

```python
from huggingface_hub import snapshot_download
from f5_tts.api import F5TTS

path = snapshot_download("mrinaltbi/tbi-tts")
tts = F5TTS(model="F5TTS_v1_Base", ckpt_file=f"{path}/model.safetensors", vocab_file=f"{path}/vocab.txt")
wav, sr, _ = tts.infer(
    ref_file="reference.wav",
    ref_text="Exact transcript of the reference clip.",
    gen_text="Text you want spoken.",
    file_wave="output.wav",
)
```

Tips: use a clean 10–20 second reference clip without background music, and write numbers and abbreviations as words.
The model uses up to 12 seconds of the clip, trimmed at a natural pause: for clips longer than 12 seconds, leave the transcript empty so it is transcribed to match; for shorter clips, give the exact transcript.

## Intended use and limitations

- **Good for:** research, demos and prototypes of narration, e-learning voice-overs, accessibility and voice assistants in non-commercial settings.
- **English only.** Other languages are not supported.
- **Output follows the reference.** Noise or music in the reference clip carries into the output.
- **Pronunciation.** Rare names, acronyms and numbers written as digits may be mispronounced.

## FAQ

**What is TBI TTS?**
An English text-to-speech model by The Brihaspati Infotech that can speak in a new voice from a 10–20 second sample.

**How much audio do I need to clone a voice?**
A single clean clip of 10–20 seconds; clips longer than 12 seconds are trimmed automatically at a natural pause. No extra training is needed.

**Does it work with Indian English accents?**
Yes. The model was fine-tuned on speakers with these accents, and our samples and benchmark use their voices.

**How fast is it?**
On an NVIDIA RTX 4060 Ti it generates speech about 4× faster than real time and needs under 2 GB of GPU memory.

**Which languages does it support?**
English.

**Can I use it commercially?**
No. The model is licensed CC BY-NC 4.0 for non-commercial use. For commercial voice projects, contact us through [our website](https://www.brihaspatitech.com/).

## About The Brihaspati Infotech

The Brihaspati Infotech builds custom speech and AI models, from data preparation to training, evaluation and deployment.
TBI TTS was trained in-house on our own GPU hardware.

Website: [www.brihaspatitech.com](https://www.brihaspatitech.com/)

It’s just warming up. --- ## မြန်မာစာ **မြန်မာစာကို အသံထွက်ဖတ်ပြမယ်။ ကြားထဲက အင်္ဂလိပ်စကားလုံးတွေကိုလည်း ဖတ်ပြနိုင်ပါတယ်။** **Howard 0.6B** ကို မိတ်ဆက်ပေးချင်ပါတယ်။ မြန်မာစာကို အသံထွက်ဖတ်ပြပြီး နေ့စဉ်စကားပြောရာမှာ ညှပ်သုံးတဲ့ အင်္ဂလိပ်စကားလုံးတွေ၊ နာမည်တွေနဲ့ စကားစုတွေကိုလည်း ဖတ်ပြနိုင်ပါတယ်။ လူတစ်ယောက်ရဲ့ အသံနမူနာ စက္ကန့်အနည်းငယ်နဲ့ အဲဒီအသံထဲက စာသားကို ပေးလိုက်ရင် စာအသစ်ကို အဲဒီအသံနဲ့ ဖတ်ပြနိုင်ပါတယ်။ *လူတစ်ယောက်လို ပြောနိုင်ဖို့ ခက်ပါတယ်။ Howard ကတော့ အခုမှ အရှိန်ရလာတာပါ။* ## Howard ဘာတွေ လုပ်ပေးနိုင်လဲ - **မြန်မာစာကို အသံထွက်ဖတ်ခြင်း** — နေ့စဉ်သုံး မြန်မာစာကို 24 kHz မိုနို အသံဖိုင်အဖြစ် ဖတ်ပြပေးပါတယ်။ - **မြန်မာ၊ အင်္ဂလိပ် ရောပြောခြင်း** — မြန်မာစာကြားထဲက အင်္ဂလိပ်စကားလုံးတွေကို အင်္ဂလိပ်လိုပဲ ဖတ်ပြပါတယ်။ - **အသံနမူနာနဲ့ ဖတ်ခြင်း** — အသံဖိုင်တိုတစ်ခုနဲ့ အဲဒီဖိုင်ထဲက စာသားအတိအကျကို ပေးလိုက်ရင် စာအသစ်ကို အဲဒီအသံနဲ့ ဖတ်ပြပါတယ်။ - **ကိုယ့်ကွန်ပျူတာပေါ်မှာပဲ သုံးနိုင်ခြင်း** — PyTorch အတွက် BF16 safetensors၊ Apple silicon အတွက် 8-bit MLX နဲ့ qwentts.cpp အတွက် GGUF ဖိုင်တွေ ပါဝင်ပါတယ်။ ## အသံကို ခွင့်ပြုချက်နဲ့သာ သုံးပါ ပြောသူရဲ့ ခွင့်ပြုချက်ရှိမှသာ သူ့အသံကို နမူနာယူပြီး သုံးပါ။ တကယ်ရှိတဲ့ လူတစ်ယောက်အဖြစ် ဟန်ဆောင်ဖို့၊ တစ်ယောက်ယောက် မပြောခဲ့တဲ့ စကားကို ပြောခဲ့သလို ဖြစ်အောင် လုပ်ဖို့နဲ့ ဘယ်သူပြောနေတာလဲဆိုတာ နားထောင်သူကို လှည့်စားဖို့ Howard ကို မသုံးပါနဲ့။ တကယ့်အသံသွင်းချက်လို့ ထင်မှတ်မှားစေနိုင်တဲ့ နေရာတွေမှာ AI နဲ့ ထုတ်ထားတဲ့ အသံဖြစ်ကြောင်း ဖော်ပြပေးပါ။ ## အသုံးပြုခွင့် Apache 2.0 လိုင်စင်နဲ့ ဖြန့်ချိထားလို့ ကိုယ်ပိုင်ပရောဂျက်တွေ၊ လေ့လာသင်ယူမှု၊ သုတေသနတွေအတွက် သုံးနိုင်ပါတယ်။ **စီးပွားရေးအတွက်လည်း အသုံးပြုနိုင်ပါတယ်။** အသေးစိတ်ကို [LICENSE](LICENSE) နဲ့ [NOTICE](NOTICE) မှာ ဖတ်နိုင်ပါတယ်။ မူရင်း Qwen ဖိုင်တွေအတွက် [မူရင်းလိုင်စင်](UPSTREAM-LICENSE.txt) က ဆက်လက်အကျုံးဝင်ပါတယ်။ Howard ကို စမ်းသုံးပေးတဲ့အတွက် ကျေးဇူးတင်ပါတယ်။ Howard က အခုမှ အရှိန်ရလာတာပါ။

# Egyptian Arabic TTS (VoxCPM2) — GGUF (BF16, Q8_0, Q4_K_M)

GGUF conversions & quantizations of [Trelis/egyptian-arabic-tts-research](https://huggingface.co/Trelis/egyptian-arabic-tts-research) (a Cairene Egyptian Arabic fine-tune of [openbmb/VoxCPM2](https://huggingface.co/openbmb/VoxCPM2)) using [llama.cpp](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp).

## Files

| File | Size | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `egyptian-arabic-tts-BF16.gguf` | 2.95 GB | Main MiniCPM4 backbone in **BF16** (full 16-bit precision) |
| `egyptian-arabic-tts-Q8_0.gguf` | 1.57 GB | Main MiniCPM4 backbone quantized to **Q8_0** (near-lossless quality) |
| `egyptian-arabic-tts-Q4_K_M.gguf` | 0.92 GB | Main MiniCPM4 backbone quantized to **Q4_K_M** (smallest & fastest) |
| `mmproj-egyptian-arabic-tts-BF16.gguf` | 2.01 GB | Required acoustic stack (LocEnc, LocDiT, residual LM in BF16) + AudioVAE (F32) |

> **Note:** All variants (`BF16`, `Q8_0`, `Q4_K_M`) require `mmproj-egyptian-arabic-tts-BF16.gguf` to generate audio.

## Usage with `llama.cpp`

Run directly from Hugging Face (`Q8_0`, `Q4_K_M`, or `BF16`):
```bash
llama-tts -hf rassmos/egyptian-arabic-tts-GGUF:Q8_0   -p "أهلاً بحضرتك، أقدر أساعدك إزاي النهارده؟"   --output out.wav
```

```bash
llama-tts -hf rassmos/egyptian-arabic-tts-GGUF:Q4_K_M   -p "أهلاً بحضرتك، أقدر أساعدك إزاي النهارده؟"   --output out.wav
```

```bash
llama-tts -hf rassmos/egyptian-arabic-tts-GGUF:BF16   -p "أهلاً بحضرتك، أقدر أساعدك إزاي النهارده؟"   --output out.wav
```

Voice cloning with a short reference audio clip:
```bash
llama-tts -hf rassmos/egyptian-arabic-tts-GGUF:Q8_0   --tts-speaker-file reference.wav   -p "أهلاً بحضرتك، أقدر أساعدك إزاي النهارده؟"   --output out.wav
```
